description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a culinary masterpiece from Oaxaca, Mexico, renowned for its incredible depth of flavor and rich, dark color. This complex sauce combines a multitude of chiles, spices, nuts, seeds, and chocolate, creating a symphony of sweet, savory, and smoky notes. It's a truly special dish, often served for celebrations, that embodies the heart of Mexican gastronomy.

instructions.title: Prepare the Chiles
instructions.text: Heat a comal or dry skillet over medium heat. Toast the chiles one by one for 30 seconds per side until fragrant, being careful not to burn them. Transfer the toasted chiles to a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them rehydrate for 20 minutes. Drain and reserve the soaking liquid.

instructions.title: Roast and Fry Aromatics and Spices
instructions.text: On the same comal, roast the tomatillos, tomatoes, onion, and unpeeled garlic until softened and slightly charred. Peel the garlic. In a separate skillet, heat a tablespoon of lard or oil. Fry the plantain slices until golden. Then, toast the almonds, pecans, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, raisins, cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, thyme, and oregano until fragrant. Fry the corn tortilla until crisp.

instructions.title: Blend the Mole Paste
instructions.text: Combine the rehydrated chiles, roasted vegetables, fried plantain, toasted nuts and seeds, raisins, spices, and crisp tortilla in a blender. Add about 1 cup of the reserved chile soaking liquid and blend until a smooth paste forms. You may need to do this in batches, adding more liquid as needed to achieve a thick, smooth consistency. Strain the paste through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl to ensure ultimate smoothness, pressing firmly to extract all liquid.

instructions.title: Cook the Mole Sauce
instructions.text: In a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of lard or oil over medium heat. Pour in the strained mole paste. Cook, stirring constantly, for at least 15-20 minutes until the mole darkens and thickens significantly, and the oil separates. This step is crucial for developing the deep flavors.

instructions.title: Simmer and Season
instructions.text: Gradually stir in the hot chicken broth, a cup at a time, incorporating it fully before adding more. Bring the mole to a gentle simmer. Add the Mexican chocolate and stir until it completely melts and is incorporated. Season with salt to taste and add the sugar to balance the flavors. Continue to simmer for at least 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, allowing the flavors to meld and the sauce to thicken to your desired consistency.

instructions.title: Serve Your Mole Negro
instructions.text: Serve the Mole Negro hot, traditionally over cooked chicken pieces or turkey, with a side of Mexican rice and warm tortillas. Garnish with a sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds. This mole can also be prepared a day in advance as the flavors deepen overnight.

tips: To achieve the deepest black color and complex flavor, toast the chiles very carefully, almost to the point of burning but not quite, and be sure to cook the mole paste for a long time in the lard until it darkens.
For an even richer flavor, use homemade chicken broth. If you cant find Pasilla Oaxaca chiles, you can substitute with more mulato or ancho chiles, but the smoky depth will be slightly different.
Mole Negro improves with age. Make it a day or two in advance and reheat gently over low heat, adding a little more broth if it has thickened too much. It freezes well for up to 3 months.
article:
Unveiling the Soul of Oaxaca: Your Guide to Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole

Few dishes encapsulate the heart and soul of Mexican cuisine quite like mole. And among the pantheon of moles, none commands as much reverence and awe as Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole. This culinary masterpiece, originating from the vibrant state of Oaxaca, is more than just a sauce; it's a symphony of flavors, a testament to culinary heritage, and a labor of love that transforms a meal into an unforgettable experience. Often served as a centerpiece for celebratory Mexican dinner recipes, learning to prepare this iconic dish is a journey into the rich tapestry of Mexican gastronomy.

## What is Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole?

Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is arguably the most complex and celebrated of all mole varieties. Hailing from Oaxaca, a region renowned for its seven distinct moles, the "black mole" stands out for its deep, dark color and incredibly intricate flavor profile. It's not merely a spicy sauce but a rich, velvety concoction made from a staggering array of ingredients – often 20 to 30 or more. The signature dark hue comes from a careful charring of specific chilies, often the chilhuacle negro, as well as the addition of dark chocolate and sometimes even toasted tortillas or bread. The flavor is a harmonious blend of sweet, savory, earthy, smoky, and subtly spicy notes, with layers revealing themselves with each mouthful. It's a dish steeped in tradition, often prepared for special occasions, holidays, and family gatherings, symbolizing a deep connection to Oaxacan culture and history.

## Ingredients You'll Need

Preparing authentic Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole requires a commitment to sourcing specific ingredients. Don't be intimidated by the list; each component plays a vital role in building the unparalleled flavor.

For the Chilies:
*   6-8 dried Chilhuacle Negro chilies (essential for authentic flavor, but can substitute with a mix of mulato and ancho if unavailable)
*   4-5 dried Mulato chilies
*   4-5 dried Ancho chilies
*   2-3 dried Pasilla Oaxaca chilies (for smoky notes)
*   2-3 dried Chipotle chilies (for subtle heat and smokiness)

For the Spices & Aromatics:
*   1 large white onion, roughly chopped
*   6-8 cloves garlic, peeled
*   2-3 ripe Roma tomatoes, roughly chopped
*   ½ cup raisins
*   ¼ cup pitted prunes
*   2 tablespoons sesame seeds
*   1 tablespoon whole black peppercorns
*   1 teaspoon whole cumin seeds
*   ½ teaspoon whole cloves
*   ½ teaspoon dried oregano (Mexican preferred)
*   ¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon
*   Pinch of anise seeds
*   Small piece of Mexican piloncillo (or dark brown sugar)

For the Nuts & Seeds:
*   ¼ cup blanched almonds
*   ¼ cup peanuts
*   ¼ cup pumpkin seeds (pepitas)
*   2 tablespoons lard or vegetable oil

For the Thickening & Darkening Agents:
*   1 small corn tortilla, torn
*   1 slice stale bread (bolillo or baguette), torn
*   2 ounces Mexican chocolate (such as Ibarra or Abuelita), roughly chopped
*   ½ cup chicken broth (plus more for thinning)
*   Salt to taste

For Serving:
*   Cooked chicken or turkey pieces
*   White rice
*   Warm corn tortillas

## Step-by-Step Instructions for Mole Negro

Making Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a multi-step process that rewards patience and attention to detail.

1.  **Prepare the Chilies:** Carefully remove stems and seeds from all dried chilies. Heat a comal or dry skillet over medium-low heat. Toast the chilies in batches, pressing them down with tongs, until aromatic and slightly pliable, about 30-60 seconds per side. Be careful not to burn them, as this will make the mole bitter. For Chilhuacle Negro, you want a deep char, almost black, but not entirely burnt. Once toasted, place chilies in a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them rehydrate for 20-30 minutes until soft.
2.  **Toast Nuts & Seeds:** In a clean dry skillet, toast the sesame seeds, almonds, peanuts, and pumpkin seeds separately until lightly golden and fragrant. Set aside.
3.  **Sauté Aromatics:** In a large skillet or Dutch oven, heat 1 tablespoon of lard or oil. Sauté the chopped onion and garlic until softened and lightly browned. Add the chopped tomatoes, raisins, and prunes, cooking until the tomatoes break down slightly.
4.  **Toast Thickening Agents:** In the same skillet, add the torn tortilla and stale bread. Toast until crispy and golden brown.
5.  **Grind the Ingredients:** Drain the rehydrated chilies, reserving the soaking liquid. In a blender, combine the softened chilies, sautéed aromatics (onion, garlic, tomatoes, raisins, prunes), toasted nuts and seeds, toasted tortilla and bread, and all the whole spices (peppercorns, cumin, cloves, anise, oregano, cinnamon). Add a little of the reserved chili soaking liquid or chicken broth to help the blades move. Blend until a very smooth paste forms. This may take several minutes and require stopping to scrape down the sides. For an extra smooth mole, strain the paste through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing firmly to extract all liquid, and discard any solids.
6.  **Cook the Mole:** Heat 1 tablespoon of lard or oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Carefully pour in the mole paste. Be prepared for it to sputter. Cook the mole, stirring constantly, for at least 30-45 minutes. This step, known as "sazonar" (seasoning), is crucial for developing the deep flavors. The mole will darken further, thicken, and take on a rich sheen.
7.  **Add Chocolate and Sweetener:** Stir in the chopped Mexican chocolate and piloncillo (or brown sugar). Continue stirring until the chocolate is fully melted and incorporated.
8.  **Simmer and Adjust Consistency:** Gradually add chicken broth, stirring constantly, until the mole reaches your desired consistency – it should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon but still flow. Bring it to a gentle simmer and cook for at least another 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, to allow the flavors to meld. Season generously with salt to taste. If it becomes too thick, add a little more broth or water.

## Pro Tips for the Best Results

*   **Source Quality Ingredients:** The unique flavor of Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole heavily relies on specific dried chilies. Seek out specialty Mexican markets for the best selection, especially for chilhuacle negro.
*   **Don't Rush the Toasting:** Each ingredient needs careful toasting to release its full aroma and flavor. Burnt chilies will ruin the mole, so keep the heat low and watch them closely.
*   **Blend Until Silky Smooth:** A smooth mole is a hallmark of a well-made one. If your blender isn't powerful enough, consider a food processor followed by a pass through a fine-mesh sieve.
*   **Sazonar is Key:** The long simmering process after adding the paste to the hot lard is essential. It cooks out raw flavors and deepens the complexity. Don't skip or shorten this step!
*   **Make Ahead:** Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole tastes even better the next day, as the flavors have more time to meld. It also freezes beautifully for up to several months.
*   **Balance Flavors:** Taste frequently throughout the cooking process. Adjust salt, and if it's too spicy, a little more chocolate or piloncillo can help balance it.

## Serving Suggestions

The traditional way to enjoy Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is spooned generously over tender pieces of chicken or turkey. It's often accompanied by fluffy white rice, which helps soak up the rich sauce, and warm corn tortillas for scooping. Beyond the classic, consider these ideas:

*   **Enmoladas:** Fill corn tortillas with shredded chicken, roll them, and smother them in warm mole.
*   **Pork or Beef:** While traditionally chicken or turkey, mole negro also pairs wonderfully with slow-cooked pork shoulder or beef short ribs.
*   **Vegetarian Option:** Serve over roasted sweet potatoes, grilled portobello mushrooms, or hearty black bean tamales.
*   **Breakfast:** A drizzle of mole over scrambled eggs can be a surprisingly delicious and indulgent start to the day.

## Variations and Substitutions

While the essence of Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole lies in its specific combination of chilies and spices, some minor adjustments can be made if certain ingredients are hard to find.

*   **Chili Substitutions:** If Chilhuacle Negro chilies are unavailable, a mix of mulato, ancho, and a small amount of pasilla Oaxaca or even a very dark guajillo can provide a similar dark color and earthy flavor. However, the unique fruitiness of the chilhuacle will be missed.
*   **Nut Allergies:** Omit specific nuts or substitute with sunflower seeds or additional pumpkin seeds if there are allergies.
*   **Vegetarian Broth:** Use vegetable broth instead of chicken broth for a vegetarian version.
*   **Spice Adjustments:** Feel free to slightly alter the amount of individual spices to suit your palate, though it's best to start with the traditional proportions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Is Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole very spicy?**
A: While it contains many chilies, Mole Negro is more about depth of flavor than intense heat. The chilies are often toasted and rehydrated, mellowing their spice, and the sweetness of the chocolate and fruits helps to balance any residual heat. It typically has a mild to medium warmth.

**Q: Can I make it vegetarian?**
A: Absolutely! Simply use vegetable broth instead of chicken broth. It pairs wonderfully with roasted vegetables, plantains, or even a hearty mushroom and potato filling for tamales.

**Q: How long does mole negro last?**
A: Stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, mole negro can last for 5-7 days. It also freezes exceptionally well for up to 3-4 months. Thaw in the refrigerator overnight and reheat gently on the stovetop, adding a splash of broth if needed.

**Q: What if I can't find specific Oaxacan chilies like Chilhuacle Negro?**
A: While Chilhuacle Negro is key to authentic Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole, a good substitute blend can be 3 parts Mulato chilies to 1 part Ancho chilies, possibly with a small amount of Pasilla Oaxaca for smokiness. Look for online specialty stores if local options are limited.

Embarking on the journey to create Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is an incredibly rewarding culinary adventure. It's a dish that speaks of tradition, patience, and the profound flavors of Mexico. While it demands time and effort, the resulting rich, complex, and utterly delicious sauce is a true testament to Oaxacan gastronomy, making it a proud centerpiece for any collection of Mexican dinner recipes. Give it a try, and taste the magic for yourself!
